### What is Skip Lot Sampling? {#sec-pmc-27}

[**Skip Lot Sampling**]{#sec-pmc-27-overview}

Skip Lot sampling means that only a fraction of the submitted lots are inspected. This mode of sampling is of the cost-saving variety in terms of time and effort. However skip-lot sampling should only be used when it has been demonstrated that the quality of the submitted product is very good.

[**Implementation of skip-lot sampling plan**]{#sec-pmc-27-implementation}

A skip-lot sampling plan is implemented as follows:

1. [Design a single sampling plan](#sec-pmc-23) by specifying the alpha and beta risks and the consumer/producer's risks. This plan is called "the reference sampling plan".
2. Start with normal lot-by-lot inspection, using the reference plan.
3. When a pre-specified number, $i$ of consecutive lots are accepted, switch to inspecting only a fraction $f$ of the lots. The selection of the members of that fraction is done at random.
4. When a lot is rejected return to normal inspection.

[**The $f$ and $i$ parameters**]{#sec-pmc-27-parameters}

The parameters $f$ and $i$ are essential to calculating the probability of acceptance for a skip-lot sampling plan. In this scheme, $i$, called the *clearance number,* is a positive integer and the sampling fraction $f$ is such that $0 < f < 1$. Hence, when $f=1$ there is no longer skip-lot sampling. The calculation of the acceptance probability for the skip-lot sampling plan is performed via the following formula

$$ P_a(f,i) = \frac{fP + (1-f)P^i}{f + (1-f)P^i} \, ,$$

where $P$ is the probability of accepting a lot with a given proportion of incoming defectives $p$, from the [OC curve](#sec-pmc-22-oc) of the single sampling plan.

The following relationships hold:

- for a given $i$, the smaller is $f$, the greater is $P_a$,
- for a given $f$, the smaller is $i$, the greater is $P_a$.

[**Illustration of a skip lot sampling plan**]{#sec-pmc-27-illustration}

An illustration of a skip-lot sampling plan is given below.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pmc-27-skip-lot
#| fig-cap: "Plot illustrating a skip-lot sampling plan for f=0.25 and i=5"
#| code-fold: true
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)

n <- 20
c <- 1
f <- 0.25
i <- 5

skip_data <- tibble(p = seq(0.01, 0.20, 0.01)) |>
  mutate(
    P = pbinom(c, n, p),
    reference = P,
    skip_lot = (f * P + (1 - f) * P^i) / (f + (1 - f) * P^i)
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(c(reference, skip_lot), names_to = "plan", values_to = "Pa")

ggplot(skip_data, aes(p, Pa, color = plan)) +
  geom_line(show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_point(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(reference = "grey40", skip_lot = "steelblue")) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.11, y = 0.75, label = "Bottom curve is (20,1) ref. plan\nf = 0.25:  i = 5", hjust = 0) +
  labs(x = "Fraction Defective", y = expression(P[a])) +
  theme_light()
```

[**ASN of skip-lot sampling plan**]{#sec-pmc-27-asn}

An important property of skip-lot sampling plans is the average sample number ([ASN](#sec-pmc-22-asn)). The ASN of a skip-lot sampling plan is

$$ \text{ASN}_{skip-lot} = (F)(\text{ASN}_{reference}) \, , $$

where $F$ is defined by

$$ F = \frac{f}{(1-f)P_i + f} \, .$$

Therefore, since $0 < F < 1$, it follows that the ASN of skip-lot sampling is smaller than the ASN of the reference sampling plan.

In summary, skip-lot sampling is preferred when the quality of the submitted lots is excellent and the supplier can demonstrate a proven track record.
